Read About Montego Bay

A name from Spanish lard-traders, a rebellion that helped end slavery in the British Caribbean, and a beach that talked the world into inventing the Caribbean vacation.

A BAY NAMED FOR LARD

Montego Bay's name has nothing to do with mangoes. Spanish settlers who held the island before the British arrived in 1655 ran a trade in pig lard out of this harbor, salting and rendering fat from the herds of wild hogs that roamed the surrounding hills for ships headed home. They called the harbor Bahía de Manteca — Bay of Lard. English settlers anglicized "manteca" into "montego," and the name stuck to the bay, then to the town that grew around it, long after the lard trade itself was forgotten.

THE REBELLION THAT SHOOK AN EMPIRE

The town square a block from St James Parish Church carries the name of Samuel Sharpe, a literate, well-traveled enslaved man and Baptist deacon who used his position as a "daddy" — an unofficial leader within the enslaved community — to organize what began as a peaceful sit-down strike over Christmas 1831. Sharpe wanted enslaved workers on Montego Bay's sugar estates to refuse work after the holiday until wages were paid. Word of the plan and rumors of freedom already granted in England spread faster than Sharpe could control, and the strike ignited into an armed uprising that swept across the parish — the largest slave rebellion in British Caribbean history, remembered in Jamaica as the Baptist War.

The rebellion was put down within weeks, but the scale of it — and the brutal reprisals that followed — shocked British public opinion and hardened the case in Parliament for abolition.

Sharpe was captured, tried, and hanged in Montego Bay's town square in May 1832. Within two years, Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act. The square where he died was renamed Sam Sharpe Square, and Jamaica later declared him one of its seven National Heroes — the only one whose defining act took place in Montego Bay itself.

THE BEACH THAT INVENTED A HOLIDAY

Long before all-inclusive resorts lined the coast east of town, a single stretch of sand did more than anywhere else in Jamaica to put the island on the tourist map. In the early 1900s, a local physician began recommending the waters off what's now Doctor's Cave Beach to patients, claiming the mineral-rich spring feeding the cove had therapeutic properties. The claim drew a stream of wealthy visitors from Britain and the United States through the 1920s and '30s, and Doctor's Cave Beach — private, reef-calmed, and photogenic — became one of the first places in the Caribbean built specifically around the idea of a beach holiday, years before the region's tourism industry existed in any organized form.

TWO CITIES, ONE HARBOR

That split origin — a working colonial port with a hard political history, and a beach resort built on leisure — still shapes how Montego Bay reads today. Downtown and the Hip Strip around Gloucester Avenue carry the older city: the parish church, the square, the harbor where cruise ships now dock. East of the airport, the resort corridor at Rose Hall and Ironshore runs almost entirely on the beach-holiday model Doctor's Cave Beach pioneered a century ago — a corridor of hotel gates and golf estates with little pedestrian connection back to the town whose name, however it started, now belongs to all of it.
